If I am given an afternoon with no particular destination, I will almost always end up walking. Not walking *to* anywhere, in the practical sense — not to the shop, not to meet someone, not in that brisk, purposeful way that makes walking merely a slower form of transport — but walking as an end in itself. There is a particular kind of thinking that only happens when the body is moving at about three miles an hour. Faster and the mind narrows to effort and breath; slower and it stalls and starts to fidget. At a walking pace, thoughts seem to loosen. They arrive uninvited and in no particular order. A half-remembered line of poetry. A decision I have been avoiding for weeks, suddenly resolving itself somewhere between one street corner and the next. The face of someone I have not thought about in ten years.

I suspect this is why so many writers, philosophers, and naturalists have been compulsive walkers. It is not romantic posturing. It is mechanics. The rhythm of footsteps gives the mind something to hold onto without requiring it to pay attention, and in that small, occupied corner, the rest of the mind is free to wander. The eye takes in hedges, washing lines, a cat watching from a wall, a particular quality of light on brick, and none of it demands anything. It just passes, and in passing, it stirs things up. Some of my clearest ideas have not come when I was sitting determinedly in front of a blank page, willing them to appear. They have come on the second mile of a walk I took specifically to avoid that blank page.

If I walk long enough in a place I know well, I start walking through time as well as space. My hometown is not an especially remarkable place — a market square, a river that floods politely most winters, streets of houses that grade slowly from old stone in the centre to newer estates at the edges — but to me every corner is laminated with earlier versions of itself. There is the bench where we used to wait after school, as if waiting itself were a social activity. There is the wall that seemed enormous when I was six and turned out, when I revisited it at twenty, to be barely waist-high. There is the shop that has been a bakery, a video rental place, a charity shop, and now a bakery again, as if the town had tried out other ideas and quietly returned to its first thought.

I find that unsettling and comforting in equal measure. Unsettling because it proves how much changes while you are not looking. Comforting because it proves how much stays. The chestnut tree by the library is still there, dropping the same impossible abundance of conkers every autumn. The shortcut through the churchyard is still quicker, and still slightly muddy even in summer. Walking those streets, I am accompanied by a crowd of former selves, all of them absolutely convinced that their version of the place was the definitive one. The twelve-year-old cannot imagine the town without the sweet shop. The twenty-year-old cannot imagine staying. The person I am now just feels affection for both of them, and a slight embarrassment at how certain they were about everything.

That is, I think, what memory actually is: not a recording, but a series of revisions we forget we have made. We tell the story of a holiday, a friendship, a failure, so many times that eventually we are not remembering the event at all. We are remembering the last time we told the story. The details polish themselves smooth with handling. The embarrassing pause disappears. The clever remark we thought of in the car on the way home migrates backwards into the conversation itself. This is not lying, exactly. It is the mind doing what it always does, which is to make a shapely narrative out of material that originally arrived as noise and weather and half-heard remarks.

There is a strange mercy in that unreliability. If we remembered everything with perfect fidelity — every slight, every awkward silence, every morning we woke up tired and disappointed for no reason — we would be crushed under the sheer inventory of being alive. Forgetting is not a defect in the system. It *is* the system. We keep what we can carry. The rest sinks, and sometimes it resurfaces years later in a smell, or a song overheard through an open window, and for a moment the past is not past at all. It is alarmingly present, more vivid than this morning, and then it recedes again. I have come to think of memory less like a library and more like a shoreline. Things wash up. Things wash away. You do not get to choose the tide.

Speaking of tides brings me, as it always does, to time itself, which I have never been able to think about for long without feeling slightly vertiginous. There is clock time, of course, the time of alarms and trains and deadlines, which expands and contracts according to mood in defiance of physics. An hour in a waiting room is not the same object as an hour with old friends. Both contain sixty minutes. They do not contain the same amount of life. And then beneath that there is deeper time, the time of geology and stars, which makes a mockery of all our arrangements. I once stood in a quarry looking at layers of rock that represented millions of years compressed into a cliff face I could touch with my hand. Each band was an era of seas rising and falling, creatures living and dying in unimaginable numbers, none of it witnessed by anything with a name for it. My entire life, laid against that cliff, would not make a layer thick enough to see.

Strangely, I do not find that thought diminishing. I find it steadying. We spend so much of our lives acting as if the present moment were the climax of history, as if our anxieties were uniquely important, our technologies uniquely transformative, our crises uniquely final. Some of them may be important — I am not arguing for indifference — but there is real relief in remembering that the earth was perfectly capable of drama long before we arrived, and that rivers will go on finding their way to the sea whether or not anyone is there to give them poetic significance. It makes my own worries smaller, but it makes my own experience more precious, too. If consciousness is rare and brief, then a Tuesday afternoon, fully noticed, is not a small thing at all.

The sea is where I go when I want to feel that scale in my body rather than just think about it. I did not grow up by the coast, which perhaps explains why I have never learned to take it for granted. People who live beside the sea develop a practical relationship with it; for me it remains slightly theatrical, in the best sense. It performs. It changes colour six times a day. It throws back the sky. There is a particular moment, just before a wave breaks, when the water rises and goes glassy and green with light inside it, and I have watched that happen hundreds of times and it has never once bored me. The repetition is the point. The sea does the same thing forever and it is never the same twice.

I like to swim in it when I can, badly and briefly, in the cold northern way that involves a lot of gasping and self-congratulation. There is no dignity in entering cold water gradually. You have to commit. And for the first minute everything in you protests, and then quite suddenly your body accepts its new situation and the cold becomes a kind of clarity. You can think of nothing else. That is a rare and valuable state. Most of modern life is the opposite: you can think of everything else, all the time, all at once, and consequently you think of nothing for very long. In cold water there is only the water, your breath, the lift of the swell, the shore looking further away than you left it. It simplifies a person, temporarily. I always come out feeling as though my mind has been rinsed.

When I am not walking or looking at water I am usually, in one way or another, dealing with words, and words are their own kind of weather system. I have always hoarded them. As a child I kept lists of words I liked for their sound alone, with no regard for whether I would ever have occasion to use them: *mellifluous, susurrus, petrichor, lambent, hullabaloo*. Some words are beautiful because of what they mean. Some are beautiful in spite of it. *Cellar door* is famous for this, but I have always had a soft spot for *dusk*, a single syllable that somehow contains the whole blue-grey hour it describes. And then there are the useful, unglamorous words that do the heavy lifting of a language without ever being praised: *almost, meanwhile, otherwise, still*.

What delights me most about language is its cheerful disobedience. We invent grammar books to restrain it, and it flows around them like water around a stone. Teenagers invent slang purely to exclude adults, and within five years the adults are using it in advertising and it dies on the spot, to be replaced by something new. Words emigrate. They take on false meanings and wear them so long the falsehood becomes truth. *Nice* once meant foolish. *Awful* once meant worthy of awe. Every time we speak, we are using a tool built by millions of anonymous people over thousands of years, most of whom had no idea they were building anything. A sentence is a collaboration with the dead. I find that thought companionable when writing is going badly, which is often. The words themselves have survived worse.

Books, for me, are where that collaboration becomes physical. I love libraries with a loyalty I cannot entirely justify on practical grounds. I know I can find almost anything faster online. I know the search function does not require me to walk across town in the rain. But a library is not really an information retrieval system. It is a place where the life of the mind has furniture. It smells of paper and wood polish and people concentrating. The particular silence of a library is unlike any other silence; it is populated. You can feel other people's attention around you like a low hum, and it makes your own attention braver.

I also love second-hand books, especially the ones with traces in them. Underlinings in pencil. A train ticket from 1987 used as a bookmark and never retrieved. Inscriptions: *To Margaret, Christmas, with love* — and then, decades later, the book in a charity shop for fifty pence, and Margaret nowhere to be found. There is an entire novel compressed into that inscription, and I will never get to read it. Someone once wrote, in the margin of a poetry collection I bought, next to a particularly gloomy poem: *cheer up!!* I think about that anonymous reader more often than I think about the poem. Reading is supposed to be a solitary activity, but books keep proving that it is not. Every used book is a small crowd.

If reading is one way of paying attention, making things is another, and lately I have become more interested in forms of making that do not involve a screen. I bake bread badly but with enthusiasm. I mend things. I have attempted, with mixed success, to learn how wood behaves, mostly by discovering the many ways it can decline to behave as I expect. There is a deep satisfaction in working with materials that have their own opinions. Dough rises or refuses to. A piece of timber splits along a grain you failed to notice. The material is not being difficult. It is being itself, and it requires you to listen before you instruct.

That is a lesson I could stand to apply elsewhere. So much of contemporary life encourages us to treat the world as infinitely editable: delete, undo, refresh, start again. Physical making restores consequence, and with consequence, care. If you cut a board too short, no menu will offer you the extra inch back. You adapt, or you start again with less wood than you had. At first this felt like a limitation. Now it feels like the source of the pleasure. The object that finally emerges — a loaf, a shelf, a mended chair — carries the history of its own corrections. It is not perfect. It is *finished*, which is a different and more honest achievement.

It is probably no accident that this interest in slow, physical things has grown as the rest of life has accelerated. My phone is a miraculous object. It contains maps of everywhere, photographs of everyone, the sum of human knowledge and also a bottomless pit of other people's opinions about breakfast. I am grateful for it and I resent it, often within the same minute. What it has really changed, I think, is not what we know but what boredom feels like. Boredom used to descend in waiting rooms and on long journeys and there was nothing to do but endure it, and in enduring it the mind would eventually, out of desperation, entertain itself. It would notice things. It would have ideas, some of them terrible, a few of them good. Now boredom lasts about four seconds before we abolish it.

I do not want to be a scold about this. I abolish my own boredom as fast as anyone. But I have started deliberately leaving gaps. I leave the phone in another room while the kettle boils. I look out of train windows instead of down, some of the time, and I am always rewarded in ways that are small and impossible to photograph well. Low sun over wet fields. A heron standing in a ditch with the immense patience of a creature that has never received a notification. Four rooks arranging themselves on a wire like notes on a stave. None of this is important content. That is exactly why it matters. A life made entirely of important content would be unbearable. We need the interstitial, unremarkable minutes. They are not the gaps in the day. Increasingly, I suspect they are the day.

Trains, in fact, are one of my favourite places to observe the unremarkable sacred. Put strangers in a carriage for two hours and a temporary civilization forms. There are treaties about armrests. There are small mercies: the offered tissue, the watched bag, the phone call taken considerately into the vestibule. There are also the great unspoken performances. The man who sighs at the exact volume that announces he is a person to whom delays happen personally. The child who stares at you with an honesty no adult would dare, until you pull a face and are rewarded with a laugh that reorganizes the mood of everyone in earshot.

I once watched an elderly woman on a train produce from her bag, with the air of a magician, a full picnic for the teenage boy opposite her, a stranger, who had mentioned to his friend on the phone that he had missed lunch. He was embarrassed and delighted in the exact proportions of a seventeen-year-old receiving unexpected kindness in public. I thought about that sandwich for weeks. Not because it was extraordinary, but because it was not. This is happening all the time, everywhere, below the level at which we usually narrate the world. We tell stories about cruelty because cruelty is news. Kindness is the weather, constant and therefore unreported, and if you start looking for it the whole climate of your day changes.

At night, when I can, I look up. I live under too much light to see the sky properly, most of the time — the stars are diluted by the orange wash of the town — but even a diluted sky is worth having, and when I find myself somewhere genuinely dark, in the hills or by the sea, I am always slightly stunned into silence, like someone who has been speaking loudly and walked into a cathedral. The Milky Way is not a metaphor down there in the dark. It is a structure. It has depth. You feel, not just know, that you are standing on a planet and looking out along the disc of a galaxy, and that the light arriving in your eyes began its journey before anyone built anything you have ever seen.

I know a handful of constellations and I am absurdly proud of them, like a man who knows six words of a language and deploys them at every opportunity. There is Orion in winter, unmistakable, the first one everyone learns. There is the Plough, wheeling around the pole through the year like the hand of a slow clock. Beyond the names, though, what moves me is the plain fact of looking. For almost all of human history, the night sky was the largest thing a person would ever see, and they saw it every clear night of their lives. They navigated by it, farmed by it, told their gods into it. We are the first generations who have been able to opt out of it. I am not sure we have gained as much from that option as we have lost.

It is getting late in this long, wandering piece, and I notice that nearly everything I have written about comes back, in the end, to attention and time: how brief we are, and how much there is to notice while we are here. The friendships that have lasted in my life are not the ones that were most intense at the start. They are the ones that accumulated. They are measured in decades of small contact — messages about nothing, the remembering of unimportant dates, the conversation that picks up mid-sentence after four months as though somebody had merely left the room to make tea. We underestimate this kind of love because it does not photograph dramatically. It has no climax. It is just there, year after year, like a well-built wall.

And the seasons keep their own slow counsel about all of this. I used to think of the year as a line, January at one end, December at the other, progress measured in what had been achieved by the time the leaves fell. More and more I think of it as a wheel. The first snowdrops are not a beginning, exactly. They are a return. The light in February has a particular thin, hopeful quality I recognize from every February I have ever lived through, and there is a deep restfulness in that repetition. Nothing in nature is embarrassed about doing the same thing again. The tree does not apologize for producing leaves identical in spirit to last year's leaves. It just gets on with it, in the faith that renewal and repetition are not opposites but partners.

So if I have a philosophy at all, after all this walking and looking and reading and making and failing to make, it is probably contained in my morning ritual, which is embarrassingly simple. I make coffee. I stand by the window while it brews. I look at whatever the morning is doing — rain stippling the glass, a blackbird deciding about the lawn, the neighbour's dog conducting its earnest inspection of the same three smells it inspected yesterday, with undiminished seriousness. I try, before the day starts making its demands, to have one minute in which I am not improving, producing, optimizing, or opining. I am just there. The coffee is hot. The light is what it is. For that minute, the world is not a problem to be solved.

Then the day begins, and I forget all of this repeatedly, and get annoyed by emails, and lose things, and check my phone while the kettle boils, and believe for whole afternoons at a time that my worth is measured by my output and other people's regard. I am not describing an achievement. I am describing an intention I renew badly, daily, the way you return to a walk you love in all weathers. Because every so often it works. Every so often I find myself — on a shoreline, in a library, on a train, at the kitchen window — paying the kind of attention that makes an ordinary moment open up like a door in a familiar wall. And on the other side of that door is the realization, always new and always obvious, that this is it. This passing, unrepeatable, mostly unremarkable day is not the rehearsal. It is the performance. The tide comes in and goes out. The rock holds its millions of years in silence. The bread rises or it doesn't. The stars continue their slow wheel whether I look up or not — but how much better it is, I keep discovering, to look up.

I know a handful of constellations and I am absurdly proud of them, like a man who knows six words of a language and deploys them at every opportunity. There is Orion in winter, unmistakable, the first one everyone learns. There is the Plough, wheeling around the pole through the year like the hand of a slow clock. Beyond the names, though, what moves me is the plain fact of looking. For almost all of human history, the night sky was the largest thing a person would ever see, and they saw it every clear night of their lives. They navigated by it, farmed by it, told their gods into it. We are the first generations who have been able to opt out of it. I am not sure we have gained as much from that option as we have lost.

It is getting late in this long, wandering piece, and I notice that nearly everything I have written about comes back, in the end, to attention and time: how brief we are, and how much there is to notice while we are here. The friendships that have lasted in my life are not the ones that were most intense at the start. They are the ones that accumulated. They are measured in decades of small contact — messages about nothing, the remembering of unimportant dates, the conversation that picks up mid-sentence after four months as though somebody had merely left the room to make tea. We underestimate this kind of love because it does not photograph dramatically. It has no climax. It is just there, year after year, like a well-built wall.

And the seasons keep their own slow counsel about all of this. I used to think of the year as a line, January at one end, December at the other, progress measured in what had been achieved by the time the leaves fell. More and more I think of it as a wheel. The first snowdrops are not a beginning, exactly. They are a return. The light in February has a particular thin, hopeful quality I recognize from every February I have ever lived through, and there is a deep restfulness in that repetition. Nothing in nature is embarrassed about doing the same thing again. The tree does not apologize for producing leaves identical in spirit to last year's leaves. It just gets on with it, in the faith that renewal and repetition are not opposites but partners.

So if I have a philosophy at all, after all this walking and looking and reading and making and failing to make, it is probably contained in my morning ritual, which is embarrassingly simple. I make coffee. I stand by the window while it brews. I look at whatever the morning is doing — rain stippling the glass, a blackbird deciding about the lawn, the neighbour's dog conducting its earnest inspection of the same three smells it inspected yesterday, with undiminished seriousness. I try, before the day starts making its demands, to have one minute in which I am not improving, producing, optimizing, or opining. I am just there. The coffee is hot. The light is what it is. For that minute, the world is not a problem to be solved.

Then the day begins, and I forget all of this repeatedly, and get annoyed by emails, and lose things, and check my phone while the kettle boils, and believe for whole afternoons at a time that my worth is measured by my output and other people's regard. I am not describing an achievement. I am describing an intention I renew badly, daily, the way you return to a walk you love in all weathers. Because every so often it works. Every so often I find myself — on a shoreline, in a library, on a train, at the kitchen window — paying the kind of attention that makes an ordinary moment open up like a door in a familiar wall. And on the other side of that door is the realization, always new and always obvious, that this is it. This passing, unrepeatable, mostly unremarkable day is not the rehearsal. It is the performance. The tide comes in and goes out. The rock holds its millions of years in silence. The bread rises or it doesn't. The stars continue their slow wheel whether I look up or not — but how much better it is, I keep discovering, to look up.
